subject_judgments.access_rationale: The delivered headings do not implement the frozen lookup routes Urban crowds, demonstrations, and popular disorder, crowd politics--1787-1788. Consequently page(s) 76, 77, 78, 82, 83 remain inaccessible for Urban crowds, demonstrations, and popular disorder: Large Paris crowds attend parlementary sessions and reinforce opposition to tax registration; Exile produces protests, clashes, anti-royal abuse, and threatened marches before troops and censorship restore temporary control; Law clerks celebrate the Paris Parlement's return even as pamphleteers condemn the compromise; Crowds surround the court during the arrest crisis, helping move the May measures to a more controlled venue; Demonstrations and riots at Bordeaux, Grenoble, Pau, and Rennes interfere directly with exile and judicial enforcement.

For Necker's public reputation and return to power in 1788, Necker, Jacques > recalls and resignations retrieves page(s) 67, 85: Public belief in Necker's earlier financial control persists and is identified as the basis for his eventual return; Brienne concludes that Necker alone retains sufficient prestige and credit to calm the markets, leading to his recall and a caretaker role before the Estates-General. No supported locator under those subject-aligned headings reaches page(s) 73, where the benchmark records Although still the public favorite, he remains personally unacceptable to the king and is briefly exiled from Paris.

The delivered headings do not implement the frozen lookup routes Law clerks, legal employment, and urban protest, law clerks--political protest. Consequently page(s) 77, 78, 83 remain inaccessible for Law clerks, legal employment, and urban protest: Paris law clerks displaced by the court's exile help lead tumultuous protests; Clerks celebrate the end of exile even as other political commentators condemn the compromise; Law clerks join students and other urban workers in prolonged street control at Rennes.

Public opinion and mass political mobilization has usable access through public opinion, political clubs on pages 75, 76, 82, but the delivered index does not retrieve the benchmark treatment on page(s) 67, 72, 73, 77, 80, 83, 84. Financial publicity, pamphlets, clubs, crowds, rumors, and public demonstrations made opinion an independent political force that ministers tried and repeatedly failed to control.

Lafayette, Gilbert du Motier, Marquis de > Assembly of Notables, Assembly of Notables supplies direct access to Lafayette's role in the Assembly of Notables on every frozen treatment page (70, 72, 74). The supported locators cover Lafayette appears among the prominent and ambitious members whom Calonne expects to manage; He later describes the Notables as lacking national representative authority while claiming a right to withhold advice without adequate accounts; He explicitly calls for a truly national assembly and identifies it with the Estates-General.

Dutch Patriot crisis and French inability to intervene is directly retrievable through Patriots (Dutch Republic); its benchmark treatments on pages 75, 77, 78 are all supported by the canonical locator audits. French support for Dutch Patriots confronted a British-backed Prussian intervention, but the fiscal crisis prevented military preparation and forced France to stand aside.

For Maupeou's 1771 judicial precedent, Maupeou, René-Nicolas de retrieves page(s) 84: Ministers recall Maupeou's tactic of dividing opposition, while markets and opponents remember the bankruptcy and reversal associated with his settlement. No supported locator under those subject-aligned headings reaches page(s) 78, 82, where the benchmark records Lamoignon considers a reform on Maupeou's scale, while Brienne initially prefers negotiation; The May judicial restructuring is presented as the monarchy's final comparable attempt to preserve absolute rule.

Calonne, Charles-Alexandre de > dismissal and exile supplies direct access to Proceedings against Calonne and his exile on every frozen treatment page (77). The supported locators cover The Parlement votes to pursue Calonne, while ministers later cancel the case after he has gone to England.

Necker's Administration des Finances of 1785 has usable access through De l'Administration des Finances (Necker) on pages 68, but the delivered index does not retrieve the benchmark treatment on page(s) 71. Necker's later financial treatise defended his own record and implicitly attacked Calonne, helping revive doubts about current borrowing and expenditure.

Turgot, Anne-Robert-Jacques supplies direct access to Turgot's fiscal warnings and opposition to American intervention on every frozen treatment page (66). The supported locators cover Turgot warns that inherited debt makes economies essential and predicts that American intervention will destroy prospects for reform; the narrative says events confirmed him.

For Parlementary constitutionalism and the fundamental laws, Parlement of Paris > constitutional declarations (1788), fundamental laws of the realm retrieves page(s) 81: The Parlement rejects the charge of judicial aristocracy and enumerates national, provincial, judicial, property, and liberty guarantees as fundamental laws. No supported locator under those subject-aligned headings reaches page(s) 80, 82, where the benchmark records The conflict after the Royal Session is framed as opposition to government by whim and arbitrary arrest; The Crown's May reforms directly attack the registration and remonstrance powers through which the court defended this constitutional role.

Stamp-duty extension is directly retrievable through stamp tax; its benchmark treatments on pages 69, 76, 78 are all supported by the canonical locator audits. The proposed extension of stamp duty became the first tax edict on which the Parlement of Paris demanded accounts and denied authority to approve a perpetual levy; Brienne later withdrew it.

For Calonne's financial administration and ministerial fall, Calonne, Charles-Alexandre de > as Comptroller-General, Calonne, Charles-Alexandre de > as Comptroller-General > and Assembly of Notables, Calonne, Charles-Alexandre de > as Comptroller-General > reform plan, Calonne, Charles-Alexandre de > dismissal and exile retrieves page(s) 68, 69, 71, 72, 73: Calonne arrives with strong court connections, favors expansive spending as a support for credit, and borrows heavily until confidence weakens; He reveals a large deficit and argues that ordinary taxation, borrowing, and economy are no longer sufficient; Enemies, distrust of his spending, and the remembered Necker surplus deprive his fiscal claims of credibility; His handling of accounts and attempts to pressure the Notables intensify scrutiny and public attacks; The public appeal fails, political rivals close in, and the king dismisses a minister no longer able to carry reform. No supported locator under those subject-aligned headings reaches page(s) 70, where the benchmark records His assumption that a handpicked assembly will endorse reform exposes limited political management skills.

Loménie de Brienne, Étienne-Charles de, Compte rendu au roi supplies direct access to Brienne's published Compte rendu of 1788 on every frozen treatment page (82, 84). The supported locators cover A newly published financial account is used to reassure readers that reform is underway before the judicial coup; Its budget assumptions fail to account for the tax arrears and fiscal disruption created by political conflict and policy reversals.

July 1788 hailstorm, harvest damage, and the fiscal shock is directly retrievable through weather; its benchmark treatments on pages 84 are all supported by the canonical locator audits. A destructive hailstorm and wider bad weather reduced expected harvests, made future peasant tax payments doubtful, and further undermined the tax-backed advances on which the treasury depended.

Assembly of Notables of 1787 is directly retrievable through Assembly of Notables, Louis XVI > and Assembly of Notables; its benchmark treatments on pages 70, 71, 72, 73, 74, 75 are all supported by the canonical locator audits. A handpicked elite assembly convened to legitimize fiscal reform instead exposed the financial crisis, challenged the government's evidence and authority, and amplified calls for national representation.

The delivered headings do not implement the frozen lookup routes Invitation for proposals on the form of the Estates-General, Estates-General--invitation for proposals, 1788. Consequently page(s) 84 remain inaccessible for Invitation for proposals on the form of the Estates-General: Brienne requests proposals and historical precedents for constituting the Estates-General, but hostile pamphleteering continues and broad design debate remains limited until the ministry falls.

For Financial transparency, accounts, and independent audit, Compte rendu au roi, Assembly of Notables, Royal Council of Finances, public opinion retrieves page(s) 67, 71, 72, 74, 82: Necker's selective public balance sheet establishes the political importance and danger of financial disclosure; Notables distrust an unsubstantiated deficit claim in light of Necker's earlier reported surplus; Disclosure of estimates and attack on the earlier accounts lead members to request still more detailed financial evidence; The Notables seek a permanent auditing commission, but Louis XVI rejects it as an intrusion on prerogative; A new official account is published to persuade the public that reform is succeeding before the May judicial changes. No supported locator under those subject-aligned headings reaches page(s) 76, 78, where the benchmark records The Parlement of Paris demands accounts before registering tax increases; Brienne responds by promising accounts and economies within a five-year recovery plan.

Parlement of Bordeaux and the provincial countermodel is directly retrievable through provincial estates, Bordeaux > parlement of; its benchmark treatments on pages 76, 77, 78, 80, 81 are all supported by the canonical locator audits. The Bordeaux court demanded stronger provincial estates, resisted vague assemblies and tax registration, endured exile, and later helped expose the weakness of nominated provincial institutions.

No delivered heading provides a realistic first lookup for Treasury suspension of payments and financial panic; the benchmark requires treatment on page(s) 85. After further advances became unavailable, the treasury suspended payments, substituted interest-bearing paper, and triggered a fall in government funds, a bank run, and an emergency political response.

Louis XVI's decisions and loss of governing authority has usable access through Louis XVI > economic and financial crisis, Louis XVI > judicial reforms and parlements, Louis XVI > and Assembly of Notables on pages 66, 70, 73, 76, 83, but the delivered index does not retrieve the benchmark treatment on page(s) 68, 74, 79, 80, 81, 82, 85. Louis XVI authorized war and successive reform strategies, protected and dismissed ministers, defended royal prerogative, imposed registrations and judicial changes, and ultimately accepted the Estates-General when credit and authority failed.

The delivered headings do not implement the frozen lookup routes Criminal-law reform as a companion to the May judicial coup, criminal-law reform--1788. Consequently page(s) 82, 83 remain inaccessible for Criminal-law reform as a companion to the May judicial coup: Measures addressing criminal-law abuses and recent miscarriages of justice precede the contentious institutional reforms to attract reform-minded support; The jurists advising on criminal reform resign in response to the wider judicial settlement, undermining the intended coalition.

Deficit, debt service, and anticipations is directly retrievable through Anticipations; its benchmark treatments on pages 69, 79, 84, 85 are all supported by the canonical locator audits. A large current deficit, debt redemption, interest charges, and extensive advances secured on future tax receipts narrowed the monarchy's options and made it acutely vulnerable to lost confidence.

The delivered headings do not implement the frozen lookup routes Military officers and the limits of coercion, army officers--political reliability, 1788. Consequently page(s) 83 remain inaccessible for Military officers and the limits of coercion: Commanders show reluctance to fire on crowds and rumors of officer hostility spread, although the narrative records no refusal of a clear order.

French intervention in the American War of Independence is directly retrievable through American War of Independence; its benchmark treatments on pages 66 are all supported by the canonical locator audits. Vergennes and Louis XVI chose covert aid, alliance, and war against Britain to exploit the colonial conflict and restore French power and prestige.

Day of Tiles at Grenoble is directly retrievable through Day of Tiles; its benchmark treatments on pages 83 are all supported by the canonical locator audits. When officials tried to exile Grenoble's magistrates, urban resistance used rooftop projectiles against troops, causing deaths and injuries and becoming a prominent symbol of provincial revolt.

Royal Session of 19 November 1787 has usable access through Royal Session (19 November 1787) on pages 79, but the delivered index does not retrieve the benchmark treatment on page(s) 80. Brienne convened an unprecedented session in the king's presence to secure authoritative support for a large loan program, but Louis XVI's order to register after free debate triggered a legality crisis.

Clerical debt and the clergy's right of self-taxation is directly retrievable through clerical debt, taxation > clerical; its benchmark treatments on pages 71, 72 are all supported by the canonical locator audits. Plans to redeem the clergy's corporate debt threatened the institutional basis of its traditional self-taxation, leading bishops to insist that only the Assembly of the Clergy could consent.

The delivered headings do not implement the frozen lookup routes Economies in the royal household and armed forces, royal household--economies. Consequently page(s) 79, 83 remain inaccessible for Economies in the royal household and armed forces: The loan plan promises rationalization of the royal household, armed forces, and financial bureaucracy; Cuts and disbandments disrupt military careers and help explain reported officer hostility and reluctance during unrest.

For Registration, remonstrance, and lit de justice, Lit de justice, Remonstrances, Parlements > powers of registration and remonstrance retrieves page(s) 76, 79, 80, 81, 82: Tax edicts move from requested registration and remonstrance to forced registration at a Versailles lit de justice; Brienne distinguishes the Royal Session from a lit de justice by allowing free opinion before the king nevertheless orders registration; The court rejects the legality of ordered registration and continues to use delays and remonstrances against royal action; The right of the parlements to register laws is incorporated into a statement of fundamental laws; The May judicial settlement seeks to remove registration and remonstrance powers from the parlements altogether. No supported locator under those subject-aligned headings reaches page(s) 77, where the benchmark records The Parlement declares forced registration illegal and directs subordinate courts not to register or publish the laws.

Mirabeau, Honoré-Gabriel Riqueti, comte de > early public and literary career supplies direct access to Mirabeau's allegations against Calonne on every frozen treatment page (72). The supported locators cover Mirabeau adds allegations of market manipulation to existing public charges of despotism, extravagance, and incompetence.

Economic liberalization in Calonne's reform program is directly retrievable through grain trade; its benchmark treatments on pages 69, 76 are all supported by the canonical locator audits. The program revived Physiocratic measures associated with Turgot by freeing the grain trade, removing internal customs barriers, and converting the corvee into a tax to stimulate prosperity and revenue.

Miromesnil's dismissal and replacement is directly retrievable through Miromesnil; its benchmark treatments on pages 73 are all supported by the canonical locator audits. Louis XVI dismissed his long-serving judicial minister during Calonne's final crisis and replaced him with the reform-minded Lamoignon.

Composition and representative ambiguity of the Assembly of Notables is directly retrievable through Assembly of Notables; its benchmark treatments on pages 70, 71, 72 are all supported by the canonical locator audits. The Assembly was dominated by nobles, clergy, magistrates, administrators, provincial representatives, and royal nominees who possessed social weight but were uncertain whom they could legitimately represent.

The delivered headings do not implement the frozen lookup routes D'Epremesnil and militant parlementary leadership, d'Epremesnil--parlementary opposition. Consequently page(s) 79, 81, 82 remain inaccessible for D'Epremesnil and militant parlementary leadership: He supports the loan program while demanding that the Estates-General meet in 1789; His motion leads to the fundamental-laws declaration, after which the king orders his arrest and he takes refuge with the court; He and Montsabert surrender only after an overnight confrontation and military encirclement.

Estates-General as the demanded and ultimately scheduled remedy has usable access through Estates-General > calls for convocation, Necker, Jacques > Estates-General and 1789 crisis, Estates-General > composition and forms (1614 vs. doubling) on pages 70, 72, 74, 75, 76, 78, 80, 81, 83, 84, 85, but the delivered index does not retrieve the benchmark treatment on page(s) 79. Once elite and judicial opponents denied the Crown's authority to create new taxes, the Estates-General became the accepted national body for consent, constitutional settlement, and recovery, culminating in a fixed meeting date for 1789.

Breton noble revolt and the deputation to Versailles is directly retrievable through noble revolt; its benchmark treatments on pages 83 are all supported by the canonical locator audits. Breton nobles organized unauthorized resistance, denounced ministers, and sent deputies toward Versailles, where the delegates were arrested and imprisoned in the Bastille.

Parlement of Paris > opposition to fiscal reforms, Parlements > political opposition and conflict > confrontations with Calonne and Brienne, Parlements > political opposition and conflict > exiles, Louis XVI > judicial reforms and parlements supplies direct access to Crown-parlement confrontation, 1787-1788 on every frozen treatment page (76, 77, 78, 80, 81, 82, 83). The supported locators cover The Parlement of Paris demands accounts, denies its ability to sanction permanent taxes, and invokes the Estates-General while rejecting key tax edicts; The court repudiates forced registration and is exiled to Troyes as the government suppresses associated political activity; Brienne negotiates a compromise that recalls the court and substitutes prolonged existing taxes for the rejected new imposts; The Royal Session dispute opens direct conflict between court and ministry and spreads resistance among provincial parlements; The Parlement of Paris articulates fundamental laws and binds itself against measures threatening its powers; Arrests and the May edicts attempt to end the courts' registration and remonstrance powers through institutional reconstruction; Provincial courts defy closure, renew demands for the Estates-General, and draw popular support against the new order.

Loménie de Brienne, Étienne-Charles de supplies direct access to Brienne's ministry and reform strategy on every frozen treatment page (73, 74, 75, 78, 79, 82, 84, 85). The supported locators cover Brienne emerges from the Notables as the plausible successor capable of carrying reform forward; He modifies the land tax and provincial assemblies, accepts the idea of audit, and ends the Assembly when royal prerogative blocks agreement; He continues a reform program amid debt redemptions and worsening international pressure; Brienne negotiates the Troyes compromise and substitutes a five-year recovery plan for the rejected new taxes; He promises a future Estates-General, new loans, economies, and a more centralized treasury while remaining confident the program can work; With Lamoignon he attempts to secure reform through a new judicial order and public-facing concessions; His effort to divide opponents and manage the future Estates-General fails while tax disorder and lender distrust empty the treasury; After payment suspension he secures Necker's return and resigns, ending the last c.

clergy (First Estate) > role in the 1788-89 political crisis, noble revolt supplies direct access to Clerical and noble resistance in 1788 on every frozen treatment page (83). The supported locators cover Provincial nobles organize unauthorized assemblies and deputations, while clergy offer little financial support and demand immediate, regular Estates-General.

Parlements > political opposition and conflict > exiles, Parlements > political opposition and conflict > confrontations with Calonne and Brienne, Louis XVI > judicial reforms and parlements supplies direct access to Provincial parlements and coordinated sovereign-court opposition on every frozen treatment page (77, 78, 80, 83). The supported locators cover Provincial courts protest the direction of royal policy and support exiled counterparts while Bordeaux is separately banished; Courts outside Paris feel betrayed by a compromise that leaves Bordeaux in exile; Provincial parlements oppose arbitrary warrants, delay taxes, demand the Estates-General, and favor stronger provincial estates; Courts defy forced vacation and mass exile, drawing demonstrations and making enforcement of the May settlement impossible.

Vingtieme taxes and their prolongation is directly retrievable through Vingtième; its benchmark treatments on pages 68, 69, 75, 78, 80 are all supported by the canonical locator audits. Wartime vingtieme taxation, its scheduled expiry, and later efforts to prolong existing levies formed a recurring bridge between debt service, reform proposals, and parlementary consent.

Necker, Jacques > Estates-General and 1789 crisis supplies direct access to Announcement of 1 May 1789 for the Estates-General on every frozen treatment page (85). The supported locators cover Brienne announces a 1 May 1789 meeting date after the treasury is denied further advances, but the markets do not respond.

Nationwide provincial and social resistance to the May Edicts has usable access through noble revolt on pages 83, but the delivered index does not retrieve the benchmark treatment on page(s) 82, 84. Sovereign and lower courts, bars, local crowds, nobles, clergy, civic groups, and some military officers resisted or obstructed the May settlement across France.

For Vergennes's foreign policy and ministerial role, Vergennes, Charles Gravier, comte de retrieves page(s) 66, 68, 70, 78: Vergennes identifies the American conflict as an opportunity to humble Britain and persuades the king to begin intervention; His support protects Calonne from court rivals while doubts about the minister's borrowing increase; His death removes Calonne's only wholehearted ministerial ally as the Assembly of Notables begins; France's inability to act in Holland is contrasted with Vergennes's earlier decisiveness and damages governmental prestige. No supported locator under those subject-aligned headings reaches page(s) 75, where the benchmark records His support for Dutch Patriots leaves successors facing possible military intervention amid an unresolved budget crisis.

The delivered headings do not implement the frozen lookup routes Royal prerogative versus permanent financial audit, royal prerogative--financial audit. Consequently page(s) 72, 74 remain inaccessible for Royal prerogative versus permanent financial audit: Incomplete and conflicting accounts lead Notables to demand stronger independent verification; The king rejects a permanent audit body as an unacceptable limitation on prerogative, after which constructive activity in the Assembly ends.

Necker's Compte rendu au roi of 1781 is directly retrievable through Compte rendu au roi, Necker, Jacques > financial management and reforms > Compte rendu au roi (1781); its benchmark treatments on pages 67, 71, 72, 73 are all supported by the canonical locator audits. The first published royal balance sheet displayed an ordinary surplus while omitting the extraordinary accounts that carried war costs, creating a durable public belief that Necker had mastered the finances.

Privilege, equality > fiscal and taxation, territorial subvention supplies direct access to Tax privilege, exemptions, and social conflict on every frozen treatment page (69, 71, 73). The supported locators cover The reform would abolish exemptions, special arrangements, and corporate privileges within a uniform land-tax system; Notables endorse equality but seek safeguards for noble and clerical representation and question the levy placed on landowners; Calonne's public appeal explicitly contrasts sacrifice by previously undertaxed interests with further burdens on ordinary people.

The delivered headings do not implement the frozen lookup routes Mass exile of provincial magistrates, provincial magistrates--mass exile. Consequently page(s) 83 remain inaccessible for Mass exile of provincial magistrates: Provincial courts that reassemble and renew demands for the Estates-General are silenced and expelled through extensive royal warrants.

Necker, Jacques > recalls and resignations supplies direct access to Necker's caretaker government and the vacuum of power on every frozen treatment page (85). The supported locators cover Necker returns after Brienne's resignation, abandons the preceding programs, and serves mainly as a caretaker while the chapter emphasizes the resulting vacuum of authority.

The delivered headings do not implement the frozen lookup routes State censorship, policing, exile, and military enforcement, government repression--1787-1788. Consequently page(s) 77, 80, 82, 83 remain inaccessible for State censorship, policing, exile, and military enforcement: Clubs are closed, booksellers constrained, troops deployed, and the Paris and Bordeaux parlements exiled as ministers restore temporary control; Royal warrants remove opposition leaders and broaden the constitutional attack on arbitrary government; Troops secure arrests and military promulgation of the May laws while courts are forced into vacation; Mass exiles and local military enforcement provoke defiance, riots, and a widening coalition against the ministry.

Civil rights for French Protestants has usable access through Protestants on pages 79, but the delivered index does not retrieve the benchmark treatment on page(s) 80. An edict granting civil rights to Protestants was introduced to create goodwill at the Royal Session, then delayed as parlementary conflict over despotism intensified.

Anglo-French Commercial Treaty of 1786 is directly retrievable through Eden Treaty, Great Britain > commercial treaty (1786) and economic conflict; its benchmark treatments on pages 69, 87 are all supported by the canonical locator audits. Whole-book synthesis: Vergennes concluded a free-trade agreement with Britain as part of an economic strategy expected to benefit French agriculture.

Lettres de cachet and freedom from arbitrary arrest has usable access through lettres de cachet on pages 80, but the delivered index does not retrieve the benchmark treatment on page(s) 81, 82. Exiles and arrests by royal warrant became a central example of despotism, prompting the parlements to claim freedom from arbitrary arrest as a fundamental right.

Territorial subvention and equality of taxation has usable access through territorial subvention on pages 69, 71, 76, 78, but the delivered index does not retrieve the benchmark treatment on page(s) 73, 74. Calonne proposed replacing complex vingtieme taxes and exemptions with a permanent land tax paid by all landowners, administered locally, and later modified by Brienne.

The Notables' qualified support for reform is directly retrievable through Assembly of Notables; its benchmark treatments on pages 71, 72, 74 are all supported by the canonical locator audits. Most Notables favored many reform principles, including tax equality and taxpayer representation, while objecting to the land tax's design, institutional safeguards, clerical provisions, insufficient accounts, and their own uncertain authority.

The delivered headings do not implement the frozen lookup routes The 420-million-livre loan program, loan program--420 million livres. Consequently page(s) 79, 80, 81 remain inaccessible for The 420-million-livre loan program: The staged loan program is designed to pay maturing short-term debts, lower advances, and support stringent economies over five years; Although the loans are registered, the legality dispute prevents the session from delivering uncontested authority; The first loan is rapidly subscribed on highly favorable terms, temporarily freeing the government to confront the parlements.

American War of Independence, Necker, Jacques > financial management and reforms > loans and war financing supplies direct access to Necker's financial administration and loan-financed war on every frozen treatment page (66, 67). The supported locators cover Necker enters office offering a less austere alternative to Turgot based on administrative reform and credit; He finances the American war mainly through heavily subscribed loans while avoiding new direct taxes and charging interest to ordinary expenditure.

Bankruptcy and collapse of the old regime in August 1788 has usable access through bankruptcy on pages 84, but the delivered index does not retrieve the benchmark treatment on page(s) 85. When lenders refused further short-term advances, the treasury suspended payments, markets panicked, Brienne resigned, and the government abandoned its reform program in favor of Necker and the coming Estates-General.

Plenary Court, grand bailliages, and the architecture of the May Edicts is directly retrievable through Plenary Court, Grand bailliages; its benchmark treatments on pages 82, 83 are all supported by the canonical locator audits. The May settlement transferred registration to a new Plenary Court, reduced parlements to appeal functions, expanded forty-seven lower courts, and suppressed offices made redundant by reduced jurisdiction.

Structural fiscal crisis of the Bourbon monarchy has usable access through monarchy > fiscal crisis and reforms, state > finances and debt on pages 75, 78, 85, but the delivered index does not retrieve the benchmark treatment on page(s) 69, 84. Accumulated debt, chronic deficits, dependence on loans and short-term advances, unequal taxation, and weak administrative control made ordinary fiscal methods increasingly untenable.

Representative consent and authority to tax is directly retrievable through Estates-General > calls for convocation; its benchmark treatments on pages 70, 72, 74, 76, 81 are all supported by the canonical locator audits. The central constitutional issue became which body could legitimately authorize permanent or new taxation and on what financial evidence such consent should rest.

The delivered headings do not implement the frozen lookup routes Public credit and confidence as instruments of royal finance, public credit--royal finances. Consequently page(s) 67, 68, 70, 74, 79, 84, 85 remain inaccessible for Public credit and confidence as instruments of royal finance: Necker deliberately links confidence in his management to the government's ability to fund extraordinary spending through loans; Calonne sustains borrowing through court-supported expenditure and favorable terms until visible doubts slow subscriptions; The Assembly of Notables is designed to create political confidence behind another round of loans; Brienne's appointment immediately improves royal credit because observers expect him to manage the Notables successfully; The November loan package succeeds initially through favorable terms and an attempted display of broad institutional support; Political disorder and uncertain tax receipts make short-term advances unattractive to financiers already threatened by administrative centralization; Markets ignore the announced Estates-General date, forcing payment suspension and a recall of the minister with the strongest personal credit.

Pau crowd's restoration of the Parlement is directly retrievable through Pau; its benchmark treatments on pages 83 are all supported by the canonical locator audits. At Pau, a crowd broke into the locked courthouse and physically restored the magistrates, directly reversing royal enforcement of the May settlement.

Necker, Jacques > recalls and resignations, Necker, Jacques > financial management and reforms > Compte rendu au roi (1781) supplies direct access to Necker's Protestant status and exclusion from the royal council on every frozen treatment page (67). The supported locators cover After his publication increases personal prestige, Necker seeks a council seat denied because of religion and resigns when the king refuses.

Anglo-French rivalry after the Seven Years War is directly retrievable through Seven Years' War; its benchmark treatments on pages 66 are all supported by the canonical locator audits. The desire to reverse the humiliation of the Seven Years War and weaken Britain's imperial power supplied the strategic and emotional setting for French intervention in America.

Rennes unrest and collapse of local authority is directly retrievable through Rennes; its benchmark treatments on pages 83 are all supported by the canonical locator audits. At Rennes, law clerks, students, and urban workers dominated the streets for weeks and expelled the intendant, exposing disagreement and hesitation within local command.

Calonne, Charles-Alexandre de > as Comptroller-General, Calonne, Charles-Alexandre de > as Comptroller-General > and Assembly of Notables, Calonne, Charles-Alexandre de > dismissal and exile supplies direct access to Court, clerical, and ministerial faction in the fall of Calonne on every frozen treatment page (68, 71, 73). The supported locators cover The queen and court favorites support Calonne's rivals, while Vergennes's patronage temporarily protects him; Personal enemies, alienated clergy, rival ministers, Necker's admirers, and Brienne's ambitions are all represented among or around the Notables; Courtiers, rivals, and ambitious successors exploit the failure of Calonne's public campaign until the king dismisses him.

For Lamoignon's judicial reform strategy, Lamoignon de Basville, Chrétien-François de retrieves page(s) 73, 78, 82, 84: Lamoignon succeeds Miromesnil with a reputation for ability and an established interest in judicial reform; He considers a Maupeou-scale settlement to break the parlements' resistance while Brienne still favors negotiation; The May program transfers registration, narrows parlementary jurisdiction, enlarges lower courts, and adds criminal-law reform; Lamoignon and Brienne attempt to outlast and divide resistance, but both fall before the public seriously turns to designing the Estates-General. No supported locator under those subject-aligned headings reaches page(s) 83, where the benchmark records Lower courts, the bar, reform jurists, and provincial tribunals refuse the new order, causing judicial paralysis.

Parlement of Paris > exile and return (1787-88), Parlements > political opposition and conflict > exiles supplies direct access to Exile of the Parlement of Paris to Troyes and negotiated return on every frozen treatment page (77, 78). The supported locators cover The court complies with exile to Troyes while public protests, repression, and provincial solidarity widen the dispute; Brienne recalls the court after it accepts prolonged existing taxes, but the compromise is widely viewed as a retreat from principle.

clergy (First Estate) > role in the 1788-89 political crisis supplies direct access to Assembly of the Clergy, don gratuit, and demand for the Estates-General on every frozen treatment page (83). The supported locators cover The clerical assembly grants little money and petitions for an immediate Estates-General followed by regular meetings.

Orléans, Louis Philippe Joseph, Duke d' supplies direct access to Duke of Orleans's legality protest and Louis XVI's reply on every frozen treatment page (80). The supported locators cover Orleans objects that ordered registration is unlawful; the king's assertion of personal will alienates the court and turns the session into a constitutional disaster.

Transformation of fiscal crisis into a crisis of political legitimacy has usable access through monarchy > absolute monarchy on pages 75, 82, but the delivered index does not retrieve the benchmark treatment on page(s) 80, 83, 85. Failed attempts to secure taxes and loans revealed that the monarchy lacked both credible accounts and accepted authority to reform, shifting conflict from finance to the constitutional basis of government.

Parlement of Paris > opposition to fiscal reforms, Parlement of Paris > constitutional declarations (1788), Parlement of Paris > exile and return (1787-88), Parlements > political opposition and conflict > exiles, Parlements > political opposition and conflict > confrontations with Calonne and Brienne supplies direct access to Parlement of Paris as center of opposition on every frozen treatment page (76, 77, 78, 79, 80, 81, 82). The supported locators cover The court rejects tax edicts, demands accounts, invokes the Estates-General, and draws conspicuous public support; It nullifies forced registration, challenges Calonne, and is exiled to Troyes; The court accepts a negotiated return and prolongation of existing taxes, attracting criticism for compromise; Brienne stages a Royal Session to obtain the court's authoritative approval for loans; The court dissociates itself from ordered loan registration and broadens its challenge to arbitrary arrest and ministerial despotism; It sets out fundamental laws, blocks tax assessments, and protects leaders sought for arrest; The Crown uses troops, arrests, and the May edicts in an effort to disable the court's obstructive powers permanently.

Calonne's Avertissement and failed appeal to public opinion has usable access through Avertissement (Calonne) on pages 73, but the delivered index does not retrieve the benchmark treatment on page(s) 72. After losing control of the Notables in private, Calonne published his proposals and portrayed resistance as privileged self-interest, attempting to mobilize public pressure behind reform.
